about: manut's one masker for token-like text: the bridge (mask_secrets), the desktop shell (tasks.rs mask_secrets) and the page (src/lib/secrets.ts) all use these patterns, and secrets.cases.json holds the table all three test against. `split` goes first: a family with a fixed body length (ghp_/gho_/ghu_/ghs_/ghr_: 36 of [A-Za-z0-9]; glpat-: 20 of [A-Za-z0-9_-]) broken by up to four line breaks or single spaces, in any letter case. Each entry is [pattern, length]; group 1 is the body's pieces, which are counted in order, and when they make exactly `length` characters at the end of a piece the prefix and those pieces are replaced by `mask` (the pieces after stay). Otherwise the text is left for `tokens`. `tokens` is replaced whole by `mask`; it also takes a token broken by line breaks or a space (up to four breaks), joining a next piece only when that piece is token-shaped (two or more capitals or digits), so a prose word after the break stays. `assigned` (case-insensitive) keeps its name and `=` and replaces the value. Item 113 added `whole`, `names` and `kept`. `whole` goes before `split`: each [pattern, flags] is replaced whole by `mask` (a private key block from its BEGIN line to its END line, or to the end of the base64 lines after it when there is no END; provider-prefixed tokens and JSON web tokens). `names` is the set of secret names that `{names}` stands for in `kept` and `assigned` (credential, token, password, passwd, passphrase, secret, api key, and access, private, secret, auth, account, client, signing, encryption or master key). `kept` goes after `tokens`: each [pattern, flags] has three groups, the first and third kept and the second replaced by `mask` (a quoted value after a secret name and `:` or `=`; a YAML line whose value is one word to the line's end, so prose after a colon stays; credentials in HTTP headers, a lone Bearer and a Cookie; the password of `scheme://user:pass@host`; `--password value` on a command line). Flags are JavaScript's (`i`, `m`); the shell builds the same with RegexBuilder, and reads `\b` as an ASCII word boundary, as JavaScript does, so a token right after Thai text is masked by both.
